Drifting the flats off Frisbees Dock and out toward the Elbow in twenty-eight to thirty-five feet, white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullets have taken fish to five and six pounds on the moving water, both stages of the tide but noticeably better on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current sweeps bait off the sandy patches near the mussel beds. It's not a doormat parade — you're culling through a lot of shorts to find keepers — but there are fish there if you keep the boat moving and stay disciplined about drifting structure edges instead of soaking in one spot.

Porgies at Shagwong and inside Fort Pond Bay have been steady on the bottom, small hooks and clam or squid strips getting bit within minutes of anchoring in fifteen to twenty feet. Nothing glamorous, but it's a good afternoon for kids and it fills a cooler when the bigger stuff is being stubborn.

The story that's got my attention for the coming weeks is offshore of all this — bluefin, schoolie class, pushing south of the Point closer than they've been in years at this point in the season. Small boats have been running out and connecting on their first tuna of the year, working bird activity and slicks a few miles off the Light. That's not something I'd have written about in a Montauk column a decade ago, but the bait's been thick enough and the water clean enough that these fish are showing earlier and closer than the old patterns suggest. Worth keeping an eye on if you've got a center console and a window of calm water — but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet. It's a bonus fish right now, not a program.

What's really going to change the complexion of the Point in the next couple weeks is what's building to our east. Squid are stacking up hard around Block Island and into Nantucket Sound as that water climbs into the high 50s and 60s in the protected coves, and that's the trigger that historically supercharges the rip bite here. When those squid schools push west and start showing in the Montauk rips — usually late July into early August — the bass that have been sulking deep in the boulder field come back up and get aggressive again, especially on the building tide at North Bar and off the Light itself.

If I had one day this week, I'd fish the Lighthouse rip on the last hour of the incoming into the first of the outgoing, working a bucktail deep and slow, and I'd have a bunker chunk rig ready as backup for Shagwong if the top-water bite doesn't materialize. This is a patient man's week at the Point. The fish are here. You just have to go down and get them.

reports.headline: Midnight Outgoing: Weakfish Under the Bridge Lights, Bass Working the Inlet Rocks
reports.subhead: The day boats have the fluke drift, but after dark is when Shinnecock really shows its hand.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night to skip the last two hours of daylight and just wait. Every July I get anglers asking why I don't fish the flood at the inlet — and every July I tell them the same thing: the bass in that rock pile want moving water and darkness, not sunshine and slack. So I sat at the jetty with a thermos of coffee until the tide turned, and by 11:45 the outgoing had built enough push to make the eels come alive on the drift. That's the window. Not sunset, not the first hour of outgoing — the meat of it, an hour to ninety minutes after the turn, when the current's ripping hard enough to hold bait against the rocks on the ocean side.

The inlet bass have been there, but they're not stupid about it. With the open ocean running warm — 71-plus out past the bar — the fish are using the inlet as a highway between the cooler, moving water inside and the bait pushing through on the tide. I've been anchoring up short of the Coast Guard station in that deep hole, 18 to 22 feet, and drifting whole and half-eels back with just enough weight to hold bottom without snagging the rip current seams. Two solid bass in the 28 to 34-inch class over the last four nights, plus a handful of shorts that came off before I could get a hand on them. It's not a blitz. It's a game of patience and staying quiet — no deck lights, no slamming hatches, just the hum of the outgoing doing the work. If you're going to fish it, fish it like you're not supposed to be there.

Ponquogue Bridge has been the more consistent story this week, and it's a night bite through and through. The pilings throw shadow lines under the sodium lights, and once that current starts running — best on the back half of the outgoing, when the flow drops but hasn't gone dead — the weakfish stack up right on the edge of light and dark. I've had guys tell me daytime jigging under there is a waste of gas in July, and this week I'd agree. After 10 p.m., though, small bucktails — quarter-ounce, white or chartreuse — tipped with a sliver of squid or a Gulp shrimp in the 3-inch size, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right along the shadow line, has been drawing weakfish in the 2 to 4-pound range, with one 6-pounder landed Thursday night that made the whole trip worth it. Keep your drag loose. Weakfish have paper mouths and this time of year the bite can be soft — more of a tick than a thump.

Daytime, the fluke drift in the bay has been fair, not great, and I'll be straight about that. The flats off Tiana and the deeper cuts toward the canal mouth are holding fish, but you're covering a lot of water for every keeper. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow over the sand-to-mud transitions in 8 to 14 feet, has been the winning combo, with fluke to 22 inches coming out of the deeper holes on the last two hours of the incoming, when the water clarifies up after the outgoing stirs the bottom. The canal itself is worth a look if you're chasing that extra push of current — the flow running down from the Peconic side has been dragging bait through, and there've been a few weakfish and short bass showing up right at the mouth where the canal dumps into the bay. It's not a secret spot, but it's underfished because most guys don't want to deal with the current there.

Bluefish have been a background character more than a headline this month. Snappers are thick in the bay — good news if you've got a kid with you and a bobber rig — but the jumbo blues have mostly stayed outside, working bait pushes past the inlet mouth early in the morning. If you want a shot at them, small metal — a Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster — worked fast at first light off the ocean side of the jetty has been the play, though I'd call that bite more opportunistic than reliable right now. Porgies inside the inlet on clam, fished tight to the rocks in 10 to 15 feet, have been steady and dependable — not exciting, but if you want a bucket of dinner fish while you wait for the tide to turn for bass, that's your move.

Looking ahead, the tides are building bigger as we push toward the next moon phase, and that usually means better current at the bridge and more consistent pushes through the inlet after dark. If that current keeps building the way I expect, I'd fish the outgoing at the inlet starting an hour after the turn, and I'd be at Ponquogue by 10 p.m. working those shadow lines on the back half of the ebb. The ocean's staying warm, which means the inside water keeps doing the heavy lifting — that's where the bait is, and that's where the fish will keep showing up. Bring bug spray. Bring patience. Leave the deck lights off.

reports.headline: The West Cut Narrowed Since the Spring Blow — Bass Are Riding the New Funnel
reports.subhead: A tighter throat at Moriches Inlet is concentrating bait and bass on the ebb, while jumbo bluefish work the boils off Cupsogue and fluke settle onto the flats.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the west jetty at Cupsogue on Tuesday's low and the sand tells a story if you know how to read it. The bar that sat off the tip back in May has migrated maybe fifteen, twenty yards closer to the rocks, and the main channel through the throat has pinched down noticeably — I'd guess it's running two, three feet shallower on the edges than it was in April. That's what a summer's worth of southerly wind swell does to this inlet. It's not a storm cut, it's a slow squeeze, sand walking in off the ocean side and stacking against the jetty face. The upshot: the current through that narrower throat is running harder than it has all season, and hard current through a tight gap means one thing on the ebb — everything gets funneled, bait and predators both, into a smaller lane than it used to be.

That's exactly what's showing up in the bass fishing. Guys working the last two hours of the outgoing off the north side of the inlet, right where the flat drops from four feet down into that 15 to 18-foot channel edge, are finding stripers stacked on the lip of that drop. Bucktails in the half-ounce to three-quarter range, white or chartreuse, cast up-current and let sink to the bottom before a slow hop back — that's putting fish in the boat, mostly slot-class fish in the 28 to 34-inch range with a scattering of shorts mixed in. After dark, the eel bite off the rocks has been the more consistent play — snake a 10 to 12-inch live eel along the current seam where the fast water meets the eddy behind the jetty rocks, let it swim naturally, and you're in business. This lines up with what's been happening farther east — heavy fish staging tight on current edges and visible boils rather than roaming open water. Moriches is doing its own version of that pattern, just on a smaller stage.

Bluefish are the wild card right now and they're not subtle about it. There's been a push of larger blues, some pushing double digits, working bunker schools that get pinned against the inlet's outer bar on the last of the ebb. If you see the water nervous and diving terns working a patch off Cupsogue, that's your window — metal, Deadly Dicks or Hopkins, worked fast through the melee. Just don't expect it to hold; these blitzes have been short and mobile, here for twenty minutes and gone. I've had two good windows this week and missed three others because I was five minutes late getting the boat turned around.

Fluke have quietly become the better bet if you want a full box rather than a highlight reel. The flats inside the inlet — from the Pattersquash side down through the deeper guts off Tuthill Point — are holding decent numbers of keeper fluke in eight to twelve feet of water. Drifting bucktails tipped with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, or a simple high-low rig with squid strips and spearing, has been the ticket on the moving tide, either direction, though the last two hours of the incoming has been putting bigger fish over the rail as bait gets pushed up onto the flats. This tracks with what's been reported up and down the South Shore and East End all month — the fluke run has genuinely improved since June, and Moriches is holding up its end. Nothing over 6 pounds that I've heard of locally, but a steady grade of 18 to 22-inch fish keeps a cooler interesting.

Weakfish are around but thin — I'm hearing occasional fish taken incidentally on soft plastics worked slow along the bay-side grass edges near Westhampton, nothing you'd plan a trip around. Porgies are filling the gap for bottom guys — the deeper holes off Smith Point and inside the bay proper are holding good numbers on sandworm and clam, standard high-low rigs, nothing fancy needed. Blackfish season's closed through the summer, so that's a fall conversation.

Water on the ocean side has stayed choppy and short-period all week — that 3 to 4-foot windswell at a quick four-second interval isn't a groundswell, it's local wind chop, and it's been enough to keep the surf grubby and limit bar access at Cupsogue to the early morning calm windows. Inside the bay, temperatures are comfortably into summer range, warm enough that the bass bite is concentrating around structure and current rather than open flats during the heat of the day. That thermal split between a churned-up ocean front and a stable, warm interior is exactly why the inlet throat has become the productive zone — it's the seam between the two systems, and seams are where fish set up shop.

Looking ahead, if the wind backs off out of the south for a stretch, I'd put my money on the dawn outgoing at the inlet for bass and blues both, working that narrowed channel edge I mentioned. If it stays blown out, shift effort inside — the fluke flats don't care much what the ocean's doing, and that's been the more dependable program the last two weeks anyway. I'd carry both game plans this weekend and let the first hour on the water decide which one you fish.

reports.headline: Forget the Wash — The Real Bite Is Behind the Jetty Rocks
reports.subhead: The ocean's a washing machine right now, so I'm working the inlet current seams — and the weakfish are finally giving me something to talk about.
reports.body_markdown:
Every guy with waders and a rod tube strapped to his back is out on the open beach right now, flogging the wash at Jones Beach like it's September. I get it — muscle memory, tradition, the whole nine. But I walked out to the water Tuesday morning, looked at that ocean, and turned right back around. Three-plus foot swell stacked up on a four-second period — that's not surf, that's a washing machine. Short, junky, close-together waves like that blow out the sandbars and scatter bait instead of pinning it. You want to soak a bucktail in that soup, be my guest. I'm fishing the rocks.

Here's the thing nobody wants to hear: the ocean side of this whole stretch, from Short Beach out past the Jones Beach water tower, has been miserable most of this week. That swell energy doesn't care about your casting arm. But flip around to the inlet side and it's a different world. Jones Inlet is doing what it always does when the front gets ugly — it's holding bait and fish in the channel and along the jetty rocks because the water's calmer, it's structured, and it's warm. I've been working the outgoing tide off the West End 2 jetty, right where the rocks meet the main channel, and that seam has been steady for stripers in the mid-20s to low 30s. White bucktail, half-ounce to an ounce depending on how hard the tide's ripping, tipped with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet, cast up-current and swung down along the rocks like you're working a river seam. Dusk into dark has been the window — that last two hours of the ebb when the sun's dropping and the current's still got some shoulder to it.

Short Beach has been quietly good too, but you have to work the back side, not the front. The sod banks along the bay side, where the marsh creeks dump out on the ebb, are pushing warm water loaded with peanut bunker straight into the inlet. Bass are stacking on those edges to ambush that bait as it gets flushed out. I had a stretch Thursday evening where three bass in a row came off a floating peanut bunker imitation worked just outside the mouth of one of those creeks — nothing giant, 24 to 28 inches, but steady, and that's more than I can say for the open beach guys I talked to at the ramp, most of whom went home with nothing.

Fluke has been a pick, not a slaughter, out in Sloop Channel. I've been drifting the deeper bend in 14 to 18 feet on the tail of the outgoing, dragging a chartreuse bucktail with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer nice and slow along bottom. For every keeper you're throwing back three or four shorts, but the ones that count have been decent — 18 to 22 inches, one five-pounder that made the trip worthwhile. If you're going to fish it, go on the last two hours of the outgoing when that current is still moving enough to keep your bait working but not so hard you're standing on 3 ounces of lead just to hold bottom.

Now here's what's actually got me fired up this week — and I don't say this lightly after years of writing this fish off. Weakfish are showing up in South Oyster Bay again, real ones, not the dink 12-inchers you catch by accident. I picked up two solid weakfish, 19 and 21 inches, working the mud flats off Cedar Creek on bucktails tipped with a squid strip, fished right at last light on the tail of the ebb when that water's calm and the current's easing off the mud bottom. It's not a blitz. I want to be straight with you — it's a handful of fish over a handful of trips, and you need to be precise about tide and light to connect. But weakfish have been ghosts in this bay for the better part of a decade, and seeing two real fish in one evening off Middle Bay mud is the kind of thing that makes an old-timer like me pay attention. If you've got a bay boat and some patience, it's worth a look right now, dusk tide, small bucktail or bare jig tipped with squid or a strip of fluke belly, worked slow right on bottom.

Blues have been mostly a bay and canal story — snapper blues are thick around the Wantagh Bridge pilings and up in the Freeport canals, little guys on tiny Kastmasters and gold spoons, good action if you've got a kid who wants bent rods all afternoon. Bigger cocktail blues have shown intermittently inside the inlet itself on bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the outgoing, but it's spotty — some days you get three, some days none.

Looking ahead: if that ocean swell settles down even a little this weekend, I'd expect some of that beach crowd to start connecting again, especially on bunker schools if they show along the outer bar. But until the period lengthens out and that washing-machine action calms, I'm staying inside — working the jetty rocks and channel edges on the ebb, and keeping an eye on those weakfish. That's where my rods are bending this week, and that's where I'd point you too.

reports.headline: Slot bass at Plum Gut — 3 A.M. and the rocks are loaded
reports.subhead: Cold water still pouring through The Race is holding bait and bass tight to the current lines while the rest of the Sound cooks.
reports.body_markdown:
Three-fifteen in the morning, standing on the rocks at Plum Gut with the tide just turning to ebb, and my rod loads up on the third cast. Slot bass, 29 inches, came off a white bucktail I was dragging through the seam where the eddy peels off the main current. That fish didn't feed soft. It hit like it meant it — and that's been the story out here all week. When the water's moving hard through the Gut and The Race, these bass are not messing around.

Here's why: New London is reading 67.5 degrees right now, a solid three to four degrees colder than Kings Point over on the west end at 71.2. That's not an accident. The Race is a funnel — millions of gallons getting rammed through a narrow slot on every tide change, and it's dragging cooler, oxygen-rich bottom water up with it. While the rest of the Sound is sliding into that flat, warm, mid-summer doldrums pattern, our water out here stays charged. Bait piles up on the edges of that cold flow, and the bass and blues know exactly where to sit and wait for it.

The pattern all week has been simple and repeatable: fish the two hours around max current, whether that's the top of the flood or the bottom of the ebb, and target the current seams — not the middle of the rip, the edges where fast water meets slower water. I've been throwing 1.5 to 2-ounce bucktails, white or chartreuse, tipped with a green Fin-S tail, letting them sink on a controlled drop off the edge of the flat before working them back with a slow, rhythmic sweep along bottom. That's put slot and overslot bass on the deck at Plum Gut and along the north side of The Race consistently — nothing giant yet, mostly 28 to 34 inches, but they're eating with purpose and there have been enough of them that I'm not calling this lucky.

Fishers Island Race has been the bluefish address. Jumbo blues, 8 to 12 pounds, blowing up on top when the bait gets pushed into the rip on the tide change. Poppers and 2-ounce Ava jigs worked fast through the boils have been getting hit almost every cast when it's happening — but it's not an all-day thing. You get a window, usually 30 to 45 minutes around max current, and then it shuts off hard until the next stage. I've run out there three times this week and connected on all three, but two of those trips I had maybe 20 minutes of real action total. You need to be on the water and ready when it turns on, not idling around hoping to stumble into it.

Fluke fishing has been fair, not great. Drifting Plum Gut and the flats off Orient Point in 40 to 60 feet, white and pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on bucktails have been picking through some keepers, but the ratio of shorts to keepers is running heavy — a lot of 14 and 15-inch fish for every one that measures. The warmer surface water is pushing bait shallower than the fluke want to sit, so the better drifts have been the deeper edges where that cold Race water is still influencing bottom temp. Porgies have been steady and reliable at Valiant Rock and Bug Light, bloodworms and clam on high-low rigs in 20 to 40 feet — not glamorous, but if you want a bent rod and dinner, that's your play right now.

Weakfish are around in small numbers, mostly as bycatch on the fluke drifts, nothing worth planning a trip around. I haven't targeted blackfish — season's closed out here through the summer, and there's nothing to report there anyway.

Night fishing off the Orient Point rocks has been my favorite session of the week. Live eels, slow-walked through the current on a fish-finder rig, into the deep water at the base of the point. That's where I got a 36-inch bass Tuesday night on the last of the ebb, and I heard of at least one bigger fish, close to 40, lost at the rocks the same night to a broken leader. If you're going to fish this spot, bring 50-pound fluorocarbon leader minimum — those rocks and that current will find any weak link in your rig.

Looking ahead, as long as that thermal gradient holds — cold Race water against the warmer Sound to the west — I expect this pattern to keep producing. The bunker schools have been building around Fishers Island, and if they push into the Gut like they did last summer, that's when this bite goes from good to genuinely dangerous for anything swimming near them. Wind's been mild out of the south, which is keeping the surface clean for now; if that holds through the weekend, I'd fish the Saturday night ebb at Plum Gut and the Sunday morning flood at The Race. If the wind swings hard out of the southwest and churns things up, I'd shift over to Fishers Island Race for the blues and save the bass fishing for the next clean tide.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Squeeze Into the Harbors — Bass and Blues Crowd the Doorways
reports.subhead: A steep temperature drop from Kings Point to New London is stacking bait tight in the western bays, and the stripers know exactly where to find the buffet.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent three mornings this week doing more watching than casting, and that's fine by me — the bait tells you everything before the rods do. Right now the peanut bunker are pushed up tight into the corners of Cold Spring Harbor and Oyster Bay, balled up so thick under the terns that the surface looks like it's simmering even though the water itself isn't doing much. Diving birds over a nervous patch of bunker in eight feet of water at first light is about as honest a signal as this Sound gives you, and this week it's been reliable almost daily inside those western harbors.

Here's why. Kings Point is reading 71 degrees, New London is sitting at 67.5 — that's a real gradient stretched across roughly seventy miles of water, and it means the western half of my beat is running warmer and holding bait tighter than the central and eastern stretches. Bunker and peanuts don't love getting flushed out into open, cooler water when there's a warm, protected pocket to sit in. So they're piling into the back bays — Huntington, Lloyd Harbor, Cold Spring, upper Oyster Bay — and the bass are following them in on the tide rather than chasing bait out on the flood the way they might in a more uniform thermal year.

The pattern that's actually working: fish the second half of the outgoing tide in those shallow, mud-bottom pockets. As the water drains off the flats it drags warmer surface water and bait with it, and that's where the current edges and seams form — right where the bass want to sit and let the buffet come to them. I've had the best luck with 3-inch white or bone Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1/2-ounce bucktails, worked slow along the drop where the mud gives way to the channel. Nothing fancy, no need to punch it far — these are close-quarters fish holding tight to structure and current breaks. Slot fish have been the bulk of it, with enough 28- to 30-inch bass mixed in to keep it interesting. A few reports of overslot fish pushing 34, 35 inches came out of the Huntington back bay complex, which tells me there's real size mixed into that bait push, not just resident schoolies.

Out on the open Sound, Stratford Shoal is still doing what it always does this time of year — concentrating everything that swims through the narrows. The rip there on the tide change has been holding bluefish, and they're not small — choppers in the 5- to 8-pound range have been busting bait on top hard enough that you can spot the blitz from a half mile off. Small poppers and 1-ounce metal, cast right into the froth on the drop, have been getting hit almost every cast when the rip is really working. Middle Ground Light has had a similar bluefish presence, though more scattered — worth a pass if you're running that direction anyway.

Fluke have been a more honest, grind-it-out story. The flats west of Port Jefferson and around the edges of Stratford Shoal in 20 to 35 feet are producing keepers, but you're working for them — a lot of shorts mixed in, and you need to cover water on the drift to find the pockets holding size. White Gulp paired with a chartreuse bucktail teaser has been my go-to, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the ebb when the current isn't ripping you off the structure too fast. Nobody's filling a cooler in twenty minutes right now, but a patient drift with bait-tipped rigs will put a few keeper fluke in the boat.

Porgies are thick around the Norwalk Islands and off Charles Island — that part hasn't changed and probably won't through August. Sandworms or clam on a simple high-low bottom rig in 15 to 25 feet on the incoming tide is still the formula, and it's about as close to a sure thing as this Sound offers right now. Weakfish have shown up as a bycatch surprise in a few of those same back-bay bass spots — nothing to plan a trip around yet, just scattered fish in the mix, which is worth noting since weakfish numbers have been thin the past few seasons.

Blackfish are off the table for now with the summer closure in effect on both sides of the Sound, so I haven't been chasing them, and neither should you.

Looking ahead, I'm watching the bait more than the forecast. If that peanut bunker push holds in the western harbors through this week's tide cycle, I'd keep working the ebb in Oyster Bay and Cold Spring Harbor — that's where the highest percentage of quality bass has been coming from. The Stratford Shoal rip should keep firing blues as long as that current keeps ripping through the narrows on the tide change; that's a spot that rewards showing up right at the turn and leaving if the boils go quiet. And I'm starting to check the sand eel situation daily now — no sign of bonito yet, but this is roughly the window when the first scouts start showing on the Norwalk Islands side most years, and the bait patterns this week suggest the Sound's getting primed for it. I wouldn't plan a trip around bonito just yet, but I'd have a light spinning rod rigged and ready before I head out.

reports.headline: Execution Rocks Ebb Puts Bass to 28 Pounds on Bunker Chunks
reports.subhead: The bunker never left Matinecock, and the bass that are stacked under them aren't leaving either — but you've got to work the tide right to get to them.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop on City Island Avenue asked me Tuesday if the bass had "moved out" of the western Sound yet, like it was already August. I laughed at him. Told him to go stand on the rocks at Execution during the last two hours of the outgoing and tell me they moved out. He came back Thursday with a 28-pound fish and didn't say much else to me, just nodded. That's how it goes out here — everybody wants to declare the season over the second the calendar flips to July, and every year the Sound tells them otherwise.

Here's what's actually happening. Kings Point buoy is reading 71.2 degrees, and that's about right for what I'm feeling off the transom — warm, comfortable, bunker-holding water from the Bridge out to Matinecock. Head east toward New London and you're down into the upper 60s, which tells you the thermal gradient across this Sound right now runs steep, west to east. That matters because it's the western end — our end — that's carrying the mature, established bite. The bunker schools that piled up off Matinecock back in June haven't broken up. If anything they've thickened, pushed by the warmth, and everywhere there's a bunker school stacked deep, there's bass underneath it working the edges on the tide change.

Execution Rocks is still the most consistent spot I've got on the board. The rockpile there does what it's always done — it breaks the current on the outgoing and creates a seam bass use to ambush bait getting swept off the shoal. I'm anchoring up-current of the light on the last two hours of the ebb, dropping bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig with 3 ounces of lead to hold bottom in 20 to 25 feet, and letting it sit. Fresh bunker beats frozen right now, no question — if you can snag a few off the surface schools before you set up, do it. Guys running live bunker on a 5/0 circle hook, lightly weighted, drifted right through that seam, are getting the bigger fish — the 28-pounder and a couple in the low 30s came off live bait, not chunks.

Stepping Stones is still doing its spring-highway thing, just slower and more tide-dependent now that we're deep into summer. Early morning, right at the top of the tide before it turns, I've had better luck there than mid-day. Bucktails — the white 1.5-ounce with a white Gulp trailer — worked slow along bottom on the drift past the light have picked at slot fish, nothing huge, mostly 26 to 30 inches, but steady enough to call it a real pattern, not a fluke.

Fluke fishing has been the honest disappointment of the week. Hempstead Harbor and the flats off Manhasset Bay are holding fish, but they're short — lots of 15 and 16 inchers, a few keepers mixed in if you cover water. I fished four drifts off Prospect Point Wednesday and only boxed one fish over 18 inches. Chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged dead slow on the last of the incoming, is still the right presentation — the fish just aren't sized up yet the way they were this time last year. If you want fluke for the table, I'd fish the deeper edges of Hempstead Harbor on a strong tide rather than wasting time on the flats right now.

Porgies have been the quiet bright spot. Execution Rocks and the rockpiles off Hart Island are loaded — small hooks, sandworms or clam, right on bottom in 15 to 25 feet, and you can fill a bucket in an hour if you've got the patience for the smaller fish mixed in. Good action for anyone bringing kids out, and a nice break from working bass structure all day.

Weakfish are showing in small numbers off Manhasset Bay and up into Little Neck — nothing to build a trip around, but if you're jigging bucktails for bass and connect with a weakfish instead, handle it gently and let it go. Numbers are still thin enough out here that I'd rather see them rebuild than end up on a stringer.

Bluefish have been a bit of a ghost this week compared to earlier in the season — I've heard of a few slammers working bait off Throgs Neck at first light, chopping bunker on top, but by the time I got out there Monday it had shut off. Worth a look at dawn if you're already headed that way, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it right now.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason for that Matinecock bunker school to break up anytime soon — the water's holding warm, the bait's thick, and the bass under it have been consistent enough three days running that I'd call it more than luck. If the wind stays out of the south and doesn't churn things up, I'd fish Execution on the outgoing again this weekend, live bunker if you can get it, chunks if you can't. Keep an eye on the tide charts — the bite windows are tightening to that last two hours of ebb, and if you show up on the wrong stage of water you'll wonder what all the fuss was about.

reports.headline: Yellowfin and early white marlin light up the eastern wall as the Gulf Stream eddy pinches Veatch and Hydrographer
reports.subhead: A warm-water push against the canyon rims has yellowfin stacked on the color, bigeye working the night chunk slick, and the first real white marlin bite of the summer showing at Oceanographer.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week gave us a decent window and I took it. Wind sat out of the southwest most days, building an afternoon sea breeze that made the run home lumpy but left the mornings flat enough to fish the troll properly. That matters more than people think — a clean morning means you can actually read the color change instead of fighting a washing-machine chop trying to find it. The moon's working through toward first quarter right now, which means the tide swing offshore is moderate, not the big springs we get around new and full. Out here that mostly shows up in how tight the eddy pinches against the canyon wall — with a softer tide push this week, the warm water has stayed pinned in against the 100-fathom curve instead of sloshing back and forth, and that's been good news for anybody running out to Veatch or Hydrographer.

What's coming this week is more of the same setup, maybe better. Water's still warming — the blue push along the eastern wall has been holding in the mid-to-upper 70s where it shoulders up against the green, and that boundary is exactly where the bite has concentrated. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't turn hard onshore, that eddy should stay locked against the rim through the weekend, which is the whole ballgame for a one-day run from Montauk. If it swings northeast, the warm water gets pushed off the edge and I'd rather stay dockside than burn fuel chasing a moving target.

Atlantis has been the most consistent of the four this past week. I ran to the 60-fathom break around 39°48'N, 71°02'W Tuesday and again Thursday, and both days the temp break was holding tight right on the edge where it drops into the canyon proper. Yellowfin in the 50-70 pound class have been eating a naked ballyhoo behind a green machine or a small Ilander/ballyhoo combo pulled at 6-7 knots, spreader bar in the shotgun position doing the real work drawing them up. Not a bonanza — I'll be honest, Tuesday we had three bites and boated two, Thursday it was five for three — but that's a respectable eastern canyon day in mid-July, and the fish have been quality, not rats.

Veatch has been the sleeper. The eddy's been sitting up on the north wall around 40°02'N, 69°24'W, and that's put a nice push of 74-degree water right up against the structure in 50 to 100 fathoms. We chunked butterfish there Wednesday afternoon into evening and connected on bigeye after dark — 120 and 140-pound class fish, both on a straight butterfly chunk with a glow stick clipped above a circle hook, baits sent back 15-20 feet under the slick with no added weight. That's a night program, not a day trip, so plan your fuel and your crew rotation accordingly if you're running from Block Island — it's roughly 90 miles out, so you're committing to an overnight unless you've got the range and the patience to run home in the dark.

Hydrographer has been quieter but not dead. The color change there has been less defined than at Veatch, more of a soft gradient than a hard rip, and the yellowfin bite reflected that — scattered, a few singles on the troll around 39°52'N, 69°00'W, nothing like the pods we found at Atlantis. Mahi have been mixed in wherever we found floating debris or lobster gear balls, nothing huge, mostly 8-15 pounders, but good eating and they'll hit a small bucktail tipped with a strip of squid or a chunk of butterfish if you cast to them instead of trolling past.

The real story this week, though, is Oceanographer, where we finally saw the first legitimate white marlin action of the season. Squid have been building around the eastern grounds — the same push that's supercharged the Rhode Island and Nantucket rips inshore has spread offshore too, and where there's squid stacked on the temp break, the billfish show up behind them. We had four white marlin bites Friday working the edge around 39°58'N, 68°08'W, converting two on ballyhoo pulled flat and dropped back on circle hooks after the fish showed on the long teasers. That's early for a big number, but it's the kind of sign that tells you the pattern's starting, not finished.

Fuel math on that run from a Rhode Island port — Point Judith out to Oceanographer is a solid 110-plus miles each way, which means you're burning the better part of your tank just getting there and back before you fish a drop of fuel on the grounds. I don't make that run unless the forecast is clean both days and the intel's fresh, because there's no cutting that trip short if the weather turns.

Looking ahead: if this southwest wind pattern holds and the eddy stays pinned against the wall like it has been, I'd put my money on Atlantis for the most reliable yellowfin troll bite and Veatch for the night chunk program on bigeye. Oceanographer's white marlin bite is the one I'm watching closest — two fish off four bites isn't a trend yet, but if the squid stay stacked out there through this week, that number should build. Either way, check the wind before you check anything else. A clean run out is worth more than any bait choice you'll make once you're on the grounds.

reports.headline: Bass Stack Up on the Southwest Ledge as Squid Push Into the Rips
reports.subhead: Warm water off the Ledge and a strengthening fluke bite give Block Island two good reasons to make the run this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the water around the island did something I like to see in mid-July — it held steady instead of crashing on us. We didn't get any big blow-through fronts, just a run of southwest breeze in the 10 to 15 knot range that kept the surface a little bumpy on the Southwest Ledge but never shut down the drift. Montauk was reading around 70 degrees, and the island's water tracks close to that number this time of year, maybe a touch warmer in the shallower rips where the sun's had all day to work on it. That's comfortable water for stripers, not the kind of heat that pushes them deep and sour. The bigger story last week was squid. Reports out of the Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound side have those concentrations building, and when squid show up in numbers around here, the rips start percolating — bass and blues key on them hard, and it's usually the first real signal that the summer pattern is locking in around the island.

This week I'm watching the tide swings more than the sky. We're coming off a moon phase that's had the currents running with authority through the North Rip and off the Ledge, and that kind of push is exactly what stacks bait against structure instead of letting it spread out over open water. As the moon eases toward the next quarter, expect the current to soften some days out and firm back up on others — when it slackens, don't stop fishing, just shift your approach. Slower current means working structure closer, not blind-casting the middle of the rip. Wind's forecast to stay in the southwest quadrant most of the week, which is livable for boat control off the Ledge but will put a chop on the surface during afternoon sea breeze — mornings and evenings are your window if you want it glass-calm.

The stripers have been on the Southwest Ledge in respectable numbers, holding in that 25 to 40-foot zone where the ledge drops off into the deeper water. I had a 40-pounder off the North Rip two weeks back on a live eel worked slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, and that pattern's held — eels drifted on a fish-finder rig or a three-way with just enough weight to stay down without dragging bottom too hard. If you're not an eel guy, umbrella rigs trolled slow through 30 to 50 feet of water off the Ledge have been putting fish in the box too, especially right at first light before the boat traffic picks up. The bite isn't a guarantee every trip — I've had mornings out there where three boats worked the same water and only one connected — but when the tide's moving right and there's bait showing on the machine, it's some of the best striper water on the whole coast right now.

Fluke have strengthened noticeably, which lines up with what I'm hearing from other boats working the drift between the Southwest Ledge and the inside grounds off Old Harbor. Four and five-pound fish aren't uncommon, and I heard of a couple pushing toward seven off a drift in 35 feet with a chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, dragged slow with the drift rather than worked hard. Squid strips on a standard fluke rig are still producing too, especially in that push of squid that's moved into the area — matching the hatch matters right now. If you're marking bait on structure but not connecting, slow the drift down. These fish are eating, but they're not chasing far for it with the water this comfortable.

Bluefish have been mixed — some days the harbor mouth and the rips off the north end have choppers in the 3 to 6-pound range slashing bait on top, other days they're absent entirely and it's all bass and fluke. When they're around, don't overthink it — a diamond jig worked with a fast retrieve or poppers at first light will draw strikes. Porgies remain a reliable backup if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating — anchor up on the rocky bottom off Southwest Point or inside the harbor breachway, small hooks, sea worms or clam, and you'll fill a cooler even on a slow bass day.

Looking ahead, I want to see how that squid push develops. If it keeps building through this week the way the regional signs suggest, the rips off the island should only get better — squid draw bait, bait draws bass, and bass on squid tend to feed hard and predictably on the tide change. My plan is to be out on the Ledge during the last two hours of the outgoing on the days the wind lets me, working eels and umbrella rigs, then shifting to the fluke drift midday when the sun's high and the bass go quiet. If the bass bite gets tougher with the softening current later in the week, I wouldn't be surprised to see more boats concentrate right on the North Rip where the depth change forces bait to hold regardless of tide strength. That's always been the fallback out here, and it rarely lets you down completely — even on a slow day, the Rip usually gives you something worth the ride.

reports.headline: School bluefin on the Mud Hole lumps as mahi start showing on the pot lines
reports.subhead: Warm blue water is pushing onto the ridge structure and the tuna bite is finally worth the run — but you still have to find the right lump.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait told the story this week. Sandeels and small bunker are pinned tight against the drop-offs on the Mud Hole lumps where the cleaner blue water is holding underneath a warm lens — and the school bluefin found them. That's a pattern I've seen a dozen Julys now: wind-driven surface warming doesn't kill the bite, it just pushes it down and tightens it up onto structure. A few days of sloppy afternoon sea breeze pushed a layer of warm, slightly dirty green water over the inshore lumps, and for a while it looked like it might shove the tuna off the structure entirely. It didn't.

This week the moon's swinging toward first quarter, which means the tide swings are moderating — not the big springs we had around the full moon, but enough push to keep bait moving off the ridges on the ebb. Wind looks like it'll lay down some mornings before the sea breeze fills in again, which is exactly the window I want. If that pattern holds, the early morning troll before 10 a.m. on the lumps should stay the most consistent play. If the breeze fires early and stays hard out of the southwest, I'd shift plans to jigging structure in closer, where the sea state doesn't matter as much.

The bluefin have been showing on the classic Mud Hole lumps — the 60 to 90 foot rises inside the Hole where the bottom breaks up sharp. Small spreads of green machines and cedar plugs, nothing fancy, pulled at 5.5 to 6 knots have been doing the damage on schoolies in the 20 to 40 pound class. When the birds are working — and they have been most mornings — I've had better luck dropping the troll gear and jigging Shimano Butterfly jigs, the 100 to 150 gram in dark green/purple, straight down through the bait ball. That's put fish in the box on days the troll went quiet by 9. Klondike has been more hit or miss — a couple boats connected on the eastern edge where it drops toward the deeper water, but the bite there has been thinner and shorter-lived than the Mud Hole. I wouldn't make Klondike your only stop right now; treat it as a secondary check on the way out or back.

Mahi are just starting to show, which tracks with what I expect this time of year — the real stacking on the pot buoys and high flyers usually doesn't peak until August, but the first scouts are already showing up on the warm-water lines pushing along Barnegat Ridge and the outer edge off Manasquan. If you find floating debris or a lobster pot line holding bait underneath, slow down and pitch a small white bucktail or a chunk of butterfish on a spinning rod before you leave it. Most of what's come over the rail so far has been schoolies in the 3 to 6 pound range, nothing to write home about yet, but the pattern is building the right way — warmer water, more current-driven debris lines, more small mahi sightings each week. By early August I'd expect that bite to turn from a curiosity into a real target.

Black sea bass remain the most dependable meat in the box right now, and the jumbos have been sitting exactly where they always sit in mid-July — deep on the wreck structure, not the open reef sand. Triple Wrecks has been the standout, sea bass to 4 and 5 pounds coming off the high structure in 110 to 140 feet on Gulp Grub/squid combos fished on a two-hook bottom rig with 6 to 8 ounces of lead depending on the drift. Sea Girt Reef and Axel Carlson have also been productive but the average size skews smaller — good numbers of keepers in the 14 to 16 inch range, with the occasional jumbo mixed in on the deeper pieces. If you're after quality over quantity, the wreck iron beats the open reef right now — the bigger fish are holding tight to vertical structure, not spread out on the sand.

Bonito have started trickling onto the shallower reef structure — Shrewsbury Rocks and the inshore end of Sea Girt Reef have both produced a few on small metal jigs and Deadly Dick lures worked fast through bait showers. It's early and scattered, more a sign of things to come than a real target yet, but worth a few casts if you're already anchored up on sea bass and see fish snapping on top.

One honest note — blackfish season is closed right now in state waters, so don't waste a trip planning around tog. That fishery comes back in the fall and it's worth the wait; the wrecks holding jumbo sea bass now are the same pieces that'll load up with big tog once the water cools and the season reopens.

Looking ahead, if the morning wind lays down like the forecast suggests, I'd be on the Mud Hole lumps at first light chasing bluefin under the birds, then working the pot lines on the way in checking for mahi. If the breeze comes up early, Plan B is simple — anchor on Triple Wrecks or Sea Girt Reef and fill the cooler with sea bass while the tuna bite sorts itself out. Either way there's enough happening on the structure right now to make the run worth it.

reports.headline: Rips fluke stack up as the drum run gives way to summer's slow-bass, hot-bite trade
reports.subhead: Doormats are stacking in the rips on the outgoing, triggerfish are eating on the reef sites, and the bass — well, they went north with everybody else's air conditioner.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Bay finally settled into its July groove. We came off a string of southwest sea breeze afternoons — 12 to 18 knots by 2 o'clock most days, glassy at dawn — and that pattern held the water clean on the ocean side even as it churned a little chop into the rips by mid-afternoon. New moon passed us on the 14th, so we're climbing out of neap water now, tides building back toward the first quarter next week. That matters more than people think: neap current in the rips means slower drift speeds, which is exactly why the fluke bite held so steady the last several days — less water moving means your bucktail stays in the strike zone longer instead of getting ripped through it.

This week we're on the building side of the cycle, current picking back up day over day into the 21st. That's going to sharpen up the rip bite — faster water stacks bait harder against the structure at Cape May Point and along the edge of the shipping channel, and it'll turn some of these lazy fluke into aggressive ones. Water's warm everywhere right now, upper 70s in the bay shallows by afternoon, mid-70s out in the rips proper. That's summer pattern water — comfortable for fluke, bluefish, and triggerfish, too warm to hold big resident stripers, which is why I want to be straight with you up front: the striper fishing here in mid-July is slow, and it's supposed to be. Most of what wintered and spring-ran through here has pushed north into cooler water. If you want linesiders right now, you're better off waiting for the fall run than beating up the rips looking for a fish that isn't home.

What is home, and eating, is fluke — and they've been good. The outgoing tide out of the Cape May Rips, working the seam where the reef structure drops off into 35 to 45 feet, has been our best water. Four-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom with just enough lift to feel the head tick sand, has been the moneymaker — I had clients into fluke to 6 pounds Tuesday working that exact drift off the Ice Breakers on the last two hours of the ebb. Don't rush the retrieve. These fish are sluggish in the heat and want it crawled, not popped. If the bucktail bite goes quiet, switch to a fluke rig with live spot or a strip of squid and just let it sit — sometimes in July that's the difference between a short and a keeper.

Hereford Inlet has been the bluefish address. Cocktail blues mixed with some genuine choppers in the 4-to-6-pound class have been blitzing bait right at the mouth on the last of the incoming, right around the jetty rocks on the north side. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks in white — thrown into the boils have been getting hit on nearly every cast when the bait's pushed up tight. That bite's tide-dependent and short — usually a 90-minute window either side of the top of the tide before the blues slide back out with the bait. Worth setting your alarm for, not worth showing up late for.

Weakfish have been a mixed bag, and I'll be honest, that's been the toughest read of the week. We're getting them in Delaware Bay proper, working the channel edges off Fortescue and down toward Egg Island, but it's been a dusk-and-dark game — small chartreuse or pink Bass Assassins on 1/4-ounce jigheads, drifted slow over the mud in 15 to 20 feet right as the sun drops. Some nights it's four or five keeper-class weakies in an hour. Other nights it's nothing and you're left wondering if you fished the wrong fifteen minutes of the tide. My honest read: the population's here, but they're not schooled up tight yet the way they can get in a good August. Patience and a thermometer app checking surface temp before you commit to a spot will save you gas.

As for the drum — that run is closed out for the season. Miah Maull, Brandywine Shoal, the mouth of the Cohansey — that whole May show wrapped up weeks ago, and there's nothing left down there worth specifically targeting drum for. If you're still hearing chatter about black drum in mid-July, somebody's telling old stories. Circle back to Fortescue and the bay flats next April.

The bright surprise this month has been triggerfish out on the reef sites — Cape May Reef and the Wildwood Reef in particular. Small pieces of clam or squid fished on light tackle right on the structure in 40 to 60 feet has been steady action, not a numbers game but a fun one, and it's a nice change of pace bite while you're anchored up waiting on a sea bass or fluke drift to develop.

Looking at this week: building tides through the 21st should sharpen the rip bite for fluke — I'd fish the last three hours of the outgoing at Cape May Point, working the deeper edge where the reef drops to 40 feet, and I'd have a bucktail and a bait rod both rigged so you can switch fast if the current picks up faster than expected. If the southwest wind holds its afternoon pattern, morning trips will stay the most comfortable and most productive — get out early, beat the chop, be off the water before the sea breeze fills in past 15 knots. For weakfish, I'd rather be wrong an hour early than late — fish the last hour of daylight into full dark at Fortescue and don't leave until you've given it a real shot on both sides of the tide change. Bass fishing, I'd sit that one out until the water starts cooling in September. Save your gas and your patience for the fish that are actually here.

reports.headline: SW wind loads the Monomoy rips, bass pinned to the seams — bonito watch is on
reports.subhead: Fluke steady on Horseshoe Shoal, stripers working the current edges at Great Point, and the first bonito scouts should be showing on the Shoals any day now.
reports.body_markdown:
We've had a week of that classic mid-July SW breeze, ten to fifteen most afternoons, and it's done exactly what it always does out here — it stacks water against the ebb at Monomoy and turns a lazy tide into a genuine current edge you can fish. Last week's new moon pushed the tides up, and we're building back toward the first quarter around the 20th, which means the range is still healthy but not the washing-machine spring tide you get around the full or new. That's a good thing right now. Big spring tides blow the bait through the rips too fast for the bass to set up on it; this in-between range lets fish hold a lane and actually work it instead of getting flushed past. Surface water in the Sound has been sitting warm — the kind of warm where you can feel it through your waders at Bass River flats by mid-morning — while the water out over the Shoals stays noticeably cooler where the upwelling keeps grinding. That gradient is the whole story of this week's fishing.

Coming into this weekend, expect the SW flow to hold most days with a light backing to south late in the week as a weak front slides through the Gulf of Maine and grazes us without doing much. Tides will keep building toward the 20th, so look for the better current on the second half of the ebb at Monomoy and the first hour of the flood at Great Point — those are the windows where the seams are sharpest and the bait gets squeezed hardest.

Stripers have been the most consistent player. Monomoy Point and the rip off the south end of the island have been holding fish on the meat of the outgoing, especially where that SW wind piles against the current and turns a soft edge into a hard one you can actually see from the boat. I've had the best luck working white and chartreuse bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounces, bounced right along the seam where the color changes from sandy tan to that deeper green — cast up-current, let it sink on a controlled fall, and work it back with the current instead of against it. Fish have been mostly schoolies and mid-twenties, but there've been enough fish pushing 34 to 36 inches mixed in to keep everyone honest. Great Point has fished a similar pattern on the early flood — sand eels are thick along that rip line right now, and a Deadly Dick or a Hogy sand eel in olive over white, worked with a stop-and-go retrieve right in the white water, has been drawing hits from both bass and some quality bluefish in the 6 to 8 pound range. Those blues have been aggressive enough that wire or at least a heavy fluoro leader is worth the trouble — I lost two good bucktails to bite-offs last Tuesday alone.

Fluke have quietly been the most dependable box-filler out here. Horseshoe Shoal and the flats off Bass River have both been holding keeper fish in that 25 to 30 foot range on sandy-mud bottom, and honestly this has been one of the better fluke stretches we've had on the Shoals side in a couple seasons. Drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, has out-produced bare bucktails two or three to one when the drift is slow — and on these building tides the drift has mostly been manageable, not the screaming current you get on the springs. Keep the rod tip low and let the bait bump bottom; most of the bites out there have been subtle thumps, not the classic slam.

Here's the part everybody's been asking me about at the dock — bonito. Not yet. I know some guys are itching, and the water's certainly warm enough in the Sound proper, but I haven't had a confirmed bonito report off Nantucket Shoals yet this season, and albies at Great Point are still a good five or six weeks out on the calendar, historically. What I am seeing that gets my attention: bay anchovies are starting to show in the pockets along the south shore and around Tuckernuck, and that's usually the leading edge of the pattern that eventually pulls bonito up onto the Shoals in late July into early August. If that bait holds and the water out over the Shoals keeps its temperature — right now it's colder than the Sound itself, which is normal for this time of year — I'd expect the first bonito scout reports within two to three weeks, probably showing first on the eastern edge of the Shoals where the cooler, cleaner water meets bait pushed off the beach.

If I had one day this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at Monomoy with bucktails, then run over to Great Point for the top of the flood and throw sand eel imitations through the rip while the light's still good. Fluke would be my backup plan if the wind lays down enough to sit comfortably on Horseshoe Shoal — that bite's been steady enough that it's hard to go wrong there even on a mediocre tide. Watch the SW wind through the weekend; if it holds in the fifteen-plus range for multiple days, the rips will keep loading up nicely, but if it swings hard south or picks up past twenty, I'd rather fish the lee side flats than fight standing water at Monomoy. Either way, keep an eye out for bait showing along the beaches — that's your first tell that the bonito switch is about to flip.

reports.headline: First bonito scouts reported off Squibnocket as Buzzards Bay rips load up with bass and blues
reports.subhead: The albies are still weeks away, but the bait's stacking in the holes and the first scattered bonito reports of the season are coming off the Vineyard's south shore.
reports.body_markdown:
Mid-July on this stretch of water is a waiting game, and this week the water gave us a hint of what's coming. We've had a stretch of settled southwest wind — nothing gale-force, just a steady 10 to 15 that's kept Vineyard Sound and the Elizabeth Islands chain from getting stirred up. That matters because clean water in the rips means the bait holds tight instead of getting scattered, and right now the bait is thick — peanut bunker pushing through Quick's Hole on the last of the ebb, silversides balling up along the Menemsha jetty at first light. The moon's working toward the new phase later this month, and as those tides build toward bigger swings, you're going to see more current volume ripping through Robinson's Hole and the Hole itself at Woods Hole — that's when the predators really start using the seams instead of just cruising them.

This week, with tides still moderate heading into the new moon build, the pattern has been about fishing the transition — the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood, when the current is strong enough to hold bait against structure but not so ripping that you can't get a lure down into the strike zone. That's exactly where the fish have been eating.

Striped bass have been the bread and butter all week, and they're sitting where you'd expect them to in mid-July — deep in the current seams off Cuttyhunk's western end, along the rocks at Tarpaulin Cove, and working the drop-off on the north side of Nashawena. Guys drifting bucktails — 1.5 to 2-ounce, white or olive, tipped with a strip of squid — through the deeper cuts on the outgoing tide have been connecting with slot fish in the high 20s to low 30s, with the occasional overslot mixed in around dawn. The retrieve that's working is Skinner's old standby: cast across the seam, let it sink dead to the bottom, then work it back slow with a lift-drop cadence that mimics a stunned baitfish rolling out of the current. Live eels fished on the drift through the Hole at night have also been productive for the bigger fish — that's still the most consistent way to find a 40-incher in this stretch, and July nights with a slack high around midnight have been the sweet spot.

Bluefish have been aggressive and reliable, which is typical for this time of year — schools ripping through Quick's Hole and the rip off West Chop chewing through anything silver. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters in the 1-ounce range — worked fast on top during the first hour of daylight have been drawing consistent strikes. Nothing subtle about it: if you see the surface nervous with bait getting pushed, that's a blitz window, and it doesn't last long, usually 20 minutes before the school moves off with the current.

Fluke fishing has been steady but not spectacular — the kind of bite where you have to put in drift time to find keeper numbers. Buzzards Bay proper, especially the flats off Wings Neck and the deeper holes inside Hadley Harbor, have given up fluke to 5 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming when the water's had a chance to warm through the afternoon sun. Scup have been thick around the Woods Hole draw bridge pilings and off the Cuttyhunk town dock — small stuff mostly, but if you want a bent rod for the kids, squid strips on a high-low rig in 15 to 20 feet has been about as close to a sure thing as this zone offers right now.

Now for the bonito — and this is the real story of the week. We've had scattered reports of the first bonito showing off Squibnocket and working the rip lines south of Menemsha on the tail end of the ebb, chasing sand eels that have been thick in that current for the last ten days. It's early, and it's not consistent yet — one solid run doesn't mean the school's parked, and I'd treat this as the opening notice rather than the invitation. If you want to chase them, small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks or Hogy epoxy jigs — cast into the rip and retrieved fast has been the ticket for the handful of fish that have come to hand. No albies yet, and I wouldn't expect them for another several weeks — that run typically doesn't fire up in earnest until the water starts easing off its summer peak in late August into September, when the bait gets pushed hard by the first cool nights. But the sand eel showing this early, combined with the bonito arriving ahead of schedule, tells me the bait cycle is running a little quicker than average this year. Worth filing away.

Looking ahead, as we build toward the new moon, expect the tidal current in Robinson's Hole and the Woods Hole passage to strengthen noticeably — bigger swings mean more water moving, which concentrates bait tighter against the ledges and makes those rips fishable for a longer window each tide, not just the peak hour. If the southwest wind holds and doesn't turn onshore and chop up the south side of the Vineyard, I'd spend my time working the bonito bite off Squibnocket on the dropping tide, with a backup plan of running to Cuttyhunk for bass if that scouting trip comes up empty. Either way, keep an eye on the bait — right now it's telling you more than any forecast will.

reports.headline: Neap tides settle the Eastern Sound bite as New London holds in the high 60s
reports.subhead: Sea bass and porgies are paying the bills at Black Point while the striper bite waits on the tide clock at Twotree Channel and Hole-in-the-Wall.
reports.body_markdown:
We're still riding the tail of that full moon push from the 10th, and it did what big July moons do to this end of the Sound — it stacked the tides high on the flood and drained them hard on the ebb, and for a few days there the current at Twotree Island Channel was ripping so much that the drift boats out of Niantic were burning through bucktails just trying to hold bottom. New London's reading around 67.8 degrees right now, which tells you this side of the Sound is still running a good four to five degrees cooler than the water piling up off Kings Point and the western end. That gradient matters — it's why our fluke bite has been more stop-and-go than the reports you're hearing out of the Norwalk and Huntington side, and it's why the sea bass and porgies, which like it a touch cooler and don't mind structure over speed, have been the more reliable meal ticket this week.

Now we're sliding into the last quarter moon, which lands mid-week, and that means neap tides settling in behind it — smaller swings, slower current, less water moving through the rips at Hole-in-the-Wall and Black Point. That's a real shift in how you need to fish these spots. On the big spring tides last week, the bass and blues were holding tight to the current lanes, using the push to ambush bait. With the current backing off, I'd expect those fish to spread out and start working the eddies and current seams instead of sitting in the main flow — which means shorter, more precise drifts and more patience at the turn of the tide rather than working the peak of the ebb or flood.

Fluke has been the mixed bag of the week. Guys drifting Niantic Bay in 18 to 25 feet on the last of the incoming have been picking at keepers, mostly 17 to 19 inches, with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow along the sandy stretches off the mouth of the Niantic River. But it's been more sorting through shorts than filling coolers — the cooler water has them a little sluggish, and the better drifts have come on days when the sun's had a few hours to warm the flats before the tide starts moving. If you're going, I'd target that midday window on the incoming rather than first light right now.

Black Point has been the more consistent producer, and it's all been about the rock piles and the reef structure just off the point in 25 to 35 feet. Sea bass have been thick there, and the party boats running out of Waterford have been putting anglers on limits of fish in the 14 to 17-inch range on squid strips and Gulp crab tipped jigs, fished tight to bottom on the slower stages of the tide when the current isn't blowing the bait off the structure. Porgies have been riding shotgun on the same drops — small hooks, sandworms or clam, and you'll fill a bucket without much drama. That bite's been steady enough that it's carrying the boats through the slower stretches on stripers and fluke.

Striped bass have been the tide-dependent story of the week. Twotree Island Channel has given up some solid fish — mid-20s to low 30s inches, with a few bigger ones mixed in — but only in tight windows around the last two hours of the outgoing, when bait gets pulled through the channel and the bass stack up on the drop-off. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig have out-produced everything else there, though a few guys working live eels along the edges at dusk have connected too. Hole-in-the-Wall has been similar — good push of bluefish mixed in with the bass on the outgoing, blitzing on peanut bunker some evenings, quiet as a church the rest of the time. It's classic ambush-point fishing: show up on the wrong tide and you'll wonder what all the talk was about, show up on the right one and it can go off fast for twenty or thirty minutes.

With neap tides settling in this week, I'm not expecting the kind of ripping current that turns Hole-in-the-Wall into a feeding frenzy — but slower water isn't necessarily bad news. It should let those bass and blues sit in the eddies longer instead of blowing through on the tide, which can actually make for a longer, more workable window if you're willing to fish it slow and let the current seams do the work instead of covering water fast. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at Twotree Channel with bunker chunks, and I'd have a Plan B lined up at Black Point for sea bass and porgies if the tide stage doesn't cooperate. McCook Point is worth a look too on the smaller tides — the current there has been gentle enough lately for porgy fishing off the beach without a boat.

Bottom line for the week: sea bass and porgies are the sure thing, fluke is a grind that rewards patience over the warmer midday tide, and stripers and blues are all about hitting Twotree and Hole-in-the-Wall on the right stage of a shrinking tide. The water's cool enough and clean enough that something's biting every day out there — you just have to be standing in the right spot when the tide says go.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:40: Bass Holding Deep, Sea Bass Filling the Cooler, Bonito Still a Rumor
reports.subhead: The rip's producing on the bottom half of the tide while everyone waits for squid to push the albies and bonito east.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack at SW Ledge ran 6:40 this morning, and I had the boat sitting over 42 feet of green water with the fishfinder with bait from the bottom third of the column right up to about 25 feet. That's the tell this time of year — when the marks are stacked mid-water instead of hugging bottom, the bass are up feeding on something other than crabs, and this week that something has been sand eels pushed tight against the ledge by the current.

I'm not going to tell you it's been easy. It hasn't. The bite at SW Ledge has been a two-hour window on either side of the tide change, and if you're not anchored up or drifting the edge precisely when that current starts to build, you're fishing empty water. Best fish have come on the last two hours of the ebb, working parachute jigs — the 4-ounce white ones — bounced off bottom and swum up through that 25 to 35 foot band where the marks show thickest. We've had stripers to 33 pounds doing that, mixed with a good number of schoolies in the mid-20s that make you think there's a bigger class of fish still staged somewhere east of us, maybe holding off Block until the water settles.

Speaking of Block — I had word of a genuinely giant bass coming off the island earlier this week, the kind of fish that reminds you why guys make the run out there in July even when the numbers aren't stacked. That's not an everyday occurrence, but it tells you the bigger migratory fish haven't abandoned the area, they're just scattered and picky. Fluke fishing off Sandy Point has actually been the more consistent producer — drifting the sand in 25 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. We've boated fluke to 6 pounds doing that drift, with decent numbers of keepers mixed with a lot of shorts that keep you busy but don't fill the cooler fast. Patience pays there — cover ground slow, feel for the bottom change where the sand gives way to broken shell, and that's usually where the bigger flatties sit.

Black sea bass have been the most dependable meat in the boat. The humps south of the Ledge, anywhere from 60 to 80 feet, are holding fish that don't care what the tide's doing — you can catch them on the slower parts of the current too, which makes them the fallback plan when the bass window closes. Green crab and squid strips on a double-hook bottom rig, dropped right to the structure, and you're not waiting long between bites. Sizes have been solid, plenty in the 16 to 18 inch range with a few pushing 20.

Now, the question everyone's been asking me at the dock: where are the bonito? Not here yet, not in numbers worth talking about. I know some of you saw a stray fish flash on the surface off North Light last week, and that's a real signal, but it's early. What's got me paying attention is the squid pushing into the Sound and up toward Nantucket water — that's the bait that usually tightens up the whole rip pattern out here. When squid concentrations build off the island, the bonito and false albacore aren't far behind, because that's the forage that draws them off the open water and into casting range at Clay Head and off the North Light rip. Right now the water temp profile still favors that happening in the next two to three weeks rather than this week — Montauk's sitting around 70, and our water off the island has been tracking close to that. Once it firms up in the high 60s to low 70s and stays there through a tide cycle, that's when I start looking for breaking fish off the rocks at first light.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely, honestly better than I expected for mid-July. Working the rip on the outgoing near SW Ledge, we've had jumbo blues in the 8 to 12 pound class hitting everything from bucktails to metal — Deadly Dicks and Ava jigs both getting bit when you work them fast through the boils. If you're getting frustrated with finicky bass, blues will save your trip and they're not shy about it.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd stick with the same pattern until something changes it — fish the SW Ledge on the last two hours of ebb for bass, work Sandy Point on the incoming for fluke, and use the humps for sea bass when the tide's dead or the wind's up. If the squid keep building around the island like they have been, I expect the albie and bonito conversation to get real fast, probably closer to the end of the month. I'll be watching the bait piles off North Light closely, and the first morning I see them nervous on the surface, that's the trip I'm calling. Until then, it's bottom bites and patience, and that giant bass off Block is proof there's still a reason to keep a rod rigged heavy just in case.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Hour Still Owns July — Bass to 28, Bluefish Chopping Higgins
reports.subhead: A slow dawn at Prouts Neck turned into the best hour of my week once the tide swung into the Pool — here's where the bite's actually happening south of Portland.
reports.body_markdown:
Threw plugs into a dead ocean at Prouts Neck for two hours Tuesday morning and had exactly one swirl to show for it. Southwest wind was light, water looked right, birds were sitting on the rocks doing nothing — and then my phone buzzed with a picture from a buddy fishing the Pool an hour later. Twenty-eight inch bass, fat as a football, taken on a chartreuse Gibbs Danny swimmer right as the tide turned and started pushing into the channel behind the Pool. That's July in Southern Maine in one sentence — you can grind out nothing for hours and then the tide flips and it's a different ocean entirely.

Biddeford Pool on the incoming remains the best hour we get down here, and this week proved it again. The bass are staging out past the bar and riding the flood in through the cut, working the edges where the sand drops into the deeper channel. I've had my best luck fishing that first hour and a half of incoming with a swimming plug — Danny-style or a Bomber Long A in bone or mackerel pattern — worked slow across the current seams. Don't horse it. Let the tide do the swimming for you and just keep the rod tip low, twitching it through the sweep. The fish holding there right now are mostly schoolies and mid-20s, but a couple guys have pulled fish into the high 20s working the last of the night tide before first light, which tells me there's a better class of bass sitting deeper in that hole than what's showing on the surface bite.

Higgins Beach has been the bluefish story all week. Peanut bunker pushed into the wash Sunday and the blues found them fast — proper blitz conditions for about forty minutes on the incoming, birds diving, fish busting bait right in the surf line. If you were there with a topwater popper — a Gibbs Pencil or a Super Strike — you had a stupid-easy hour. I heard from two separate guys who limited out on cocktail blues in that window and one who stuck a bigger fish, six or seven pounds, on a bucktail he happened to have tied on. That bunker school has been moving up and down the beach, not locked into one spot, so if you're headed to Higgins right now, walk the beach and watch for the diving terns before you commit to a spot. When the birds go quiet, so does the bite — it shuts off almost as fast as it turns on.

Pine Point and the Scarborough River marsh have been slower and more of a grind, which is normal for mid-July once the water in there gets skinny and warm on the low. I fished the outgoing there Wednesday evening and picked at schoolie bass working the mouth where the river dumps out past the flats — small profile soft plastics, 4-inch white Slug-Go on a light jighead, worked slow along the channel edge. Nothing big, but steady enough to keep you interested for an hour around sunset. If you want flounder, that same stretch and the channels off Wells Harbor have been giving up decent numbers on bloodworms and squid strips fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, bounced slow along the mud on the bottom of the tide.

Mackerel showed up off the Wells Harbor jetty and out toward Cape Neddick this week in decent numbers — good sign for the fall run later on, and a great source of fresh bait right now if you want to switch off dead bunker chunks. A Sabiki rig dropped straight down off the jetty rocks on the last two hours of the incoming has been filling coolers fast, and a live mackerel drifted out past the rocks at Prouts Neck or Cape Elizabeth is about as good a bass bait as exists this time of year — I'd rather fish one live mack under a balloon than chuck plugs blind on a slow tide.

Prouts Neck itself has been up and down depending on the wind. When it's blowing out of the southwest like it did Tuesday, that side sets up calm and clean, and the bass push in tight to the rocks on the last two hours of the flood — but you need moving water and the right wind together, and this week we only had one without the other most days.
